query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (density < 6 g/cm³), a controlled post-processing thermal treatment (with defined cooling/annealing cycles) will induce a transformation from a mixture of metastable intermetallic precipitates and solid solution regions into a more homogenized microstructure that is enriched at the surface in Al (and possibly other protective elements). This refined phase distribution promotes the in situ formation of a continuous and adherent oxide film when exposed to corrosive media and high-temperature oxidizing environments, thereby enhancing both corrosion resistance and oxidation stability relative to baseline alloys processed by isotropic cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy containing mixed metastable phases (solid solutions and intermetallic compounds) produced via induction melting.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-processing thermal treatment with controlled cooling rates and annealing cycles to promote phase transformation, followed by environmental exposure under aggressive corrosive electrolytes and high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.conditions: Annealing under non-equilibrium conditions (ambient to high temperatures with defined hold and cooling periods) followed by comparative tests in standardized corrosive environments (e.g., electrochemical cells) and oxidation tests at temperatures up to approximately 900 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of the initial metastable microstructure into a homogenized phase distribution with a refined, Al-enriched intermetallic/solid solution phase along grain boundaries and surfaces, which facilitates the nucleation and growth of a continuous protective oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment accelerates phase transformation kinetics such that unstable intermetallic precipitates dissolve or re-precipitate in a refined manner, altering interfacial chemistry. This results in an enhanced segregation of elements (e.g., Al) at the surface that, upon exposure to oxidizing conditions, forms a dense and adherent oxide film that effectively retards corrosive attack and scale spallation at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline processing route (isotropic cooling without tailored treatment), the thermally treated alloy is expected to show a lower corrosion current density and higher corrosion potential in electrochemical tests, a reduced mass change during high-temperature oxidation tests, and microstructural evidence (by XRD/SEM) of a continuous, adherent oxide scale.
generation.baseline: Identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy processed using standard, isotropic cooling, without the controlled post-processing thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the compositional and density constraints (density < 6 g/cm³) and under environmental test conditions that simulate moderate corrosive media and high-temperature (up to ~900 °C) oxidation; it assumes similar alloy compositions and that other processing variables remain constant.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the phase transformations and the precise composition and thickness of the protective oxide scale are not fully predictable without further experimental evidence. Additionally, the quantitative improvement in corrosion and oxidation behavior depends on the fine-tuning of the thermal treatment parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples. Process one set using a controlled post-processing thermal treatment (with specified cooling/annealing cycles) to induce the hypothesized phase transformation, while processing the control set via standard isotropic cooling. Subsequently, subject both sets to identical corrosive media exposure (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) and high-temperature oxidation tests (up to ~900 °C), and then compare their microstructural evolution via XRD/SEM.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to measure corrosion current density and corrosion potential
Mass change measurements during high-temperature oxidation
XRD and SEM analyses before and after exposure to assess phase evolution and the formation/adherence of the protective oxide scale
Surface chemical analysis (EDS) to confirm enrichment of protective elements (e.g., Al) in the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal treatment does not result in statistically significant improvements—namely, if the treated samples do not display lower corrosion current densities, higher corrosion potentials, reduced mass loss during oxidation, and evidence of a continuous protective oxide scale compared to the baseline samples—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.
